Where it began

Murali Vijay was born in Madras (the city that became Chennai) on 1 April 1984. He came to serious cricket fairly late, taking up the college game at 17, and was spotted there by the former India player Bharat Arun. From the Tamil Nadu under-22 side he moved into the Ranji Trophy, and his first season, 2006–07, went about as well as a first season can: a fifty on debut against Delhi, two hundreds and 628 runs, third best in the whole competition.

The next winter he made 230 not out against Saurashtra and put on 462 for the first wicket with Abhinav Mukund, a stand that missed the Indian first-class record by a mere two runs. Selectors started writing his name down.

The player

His Test call came in November 2008, so suddenly that he was taken out of a Ranji match to make his debut against Australia at Nagpur. He made 33 and 41, shared two solid opening stands with Virender Sehwag and ran out both Matthew Hayden and Michael Hussey. His first Test hundred, 139 against Australia at Bangalore, followed in 2010.

His best years began in 2013, when he came back against Australia with hundreds in consecutive Tests and finished as the leading scorer of the series. In England in 2014 he again topped the scoring, and at Brisbane that winter his 144 equalled the highest score by an Indian on the ground. In all he played 61 Tests between 2008 and 2018 and made 3,982 runs at 38.29, with 12 hundreds, 15 fifties and a best of 167. He also held 49 catches.

What made him special

Patience. Vijay could bat through long sessions without his concentration slipping, which earned him the nickname The Monk. He leaned into the ball off the front foot and timed it with his wrists, a method that reminded some people of VVS Laxman. Away from home, on bouncier pitches, he stood tall and played the ball late, and he enjoyed himself against spin. Then, just when a bowler thought he was settled in for a quiet day, he would loft one over the infield.

The one-day game never quite took to him the way Tests did, and he played only 17 one-day internationals. An opener built for long days can perhaps be forgiven for finding fifty overs a little short.

Away from the middle

In the Indian Premier League he was a key batter for his home side, Chennai Super Kings, when they won the title in 2010 and 2011, making 458 runs in the first of those seasons. He was also the leading run-scorer as Chennai won the 2010 Champions League Twenty20. Later he captained Kings XI Punjab, and he led Kovai Kings in the first two seasons of the Tamil Nadu Premier League. He retired from all cricket in January 2023, with more than 13,000 runs across every form of the game.

And finally

His off-breaks brought him exactly one Test wicket, at a cost of 198 runs. Few wickets in the history of the game have been waited for so patiently, which seems only right for The Monk.
